newsitem.title: UK: Rushdie supporters welcome EU moves against Iran.
newsitem.headline: Rushdie supporters welcome EU moves against Iran.

text.p: Supporters of death threat author Salman Rushdie welcomed a decision by EU nations to withdraw ambassadors from Tehran after a German court ruled that Iranian leaders had sanctioned the killing of Kurdish leaders.

"We are very pleased that the efforts to silence the German prosecutors have not worked. Terrorism in Europe perpetrated by Iran has been going on for many, many years," Frances D'Souza, the chair of the International Rushdie defence committees, told Reuters.
"Most governments have known about it and have condoned it because it hasn't been made public. Now it has been made public and all the governments are reacting."
DeSouza spoke to Rushdie on Thursday after the German court found Iranian political leaders had ordered the killings of a group of Iranian Kurdish leaders in a Berlin restaurant in 1992.
She said the Indian-born, British author believes it could be an important first step in the eventual lifting of the Iranian-imposed death threat against him.
"He's obviously very pleased because the kind of terrorism under which he has had to live for eight years has finally been acknowledged."
Iran's late spiritual leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomenei ordered Rushdie's killing in 1989 following the publication of his novel "The Satanic Verses" which was deemed blasphemous to Islam.
Despite her relief, DeSouza's optimism was tempered by a fear that the EU move will be only a gesture and not a real attempt to confront terrorism in the heart of Europe.
"That is my greatest fear," she said. "We will try to see that there are lasting benefits."

As executive director of the human rights pressure group Article 19, D'Souza has written to the president of the Council of Ministers of Europe urging him to start discussions within Europe about sanctions against Iran.
"The only way in order to make it quite clear to Iran that you mean business and that you will not tolerate terrorism anymore is by discussing sanctions," she said.
Perhaps the most important implication of the German court ruling, she added, was that it now forces nations to deal with the problem of terrorism.

Although the Iranian president and religious leaders have only been implicated and not named in the ruling, D'Souza believes it will only be a matter of time before they will be. "What the court has done is sufficient to make it impossible for the Iranians to wriggle out of it, she said.
As for Rushdie, the decision is very good news. His supporters felt European nations had used the critical dialogue with Iran as an excuse to do nothing.
"Now they don't have that excuse anymore. Now they have to do someting, or something different," D'Souza added.
